chapters.s: “The brighter the seal shines, the denser the darkness inside the cover.” After that night, when the coconut leaf floated over the black river without sinking, no one in Channa Grove slept well. But the mark did not dry. Until dawn a name kept glimmering inside it.

chapters.s: “When a name returns home, even the soil wakes from its sleep.” “When a name comes home, the earth too awakens.” When the first bird called at dawn, no one in Garh Narikel heard it as an ordinary bird. Its call sounded like an announcement. The court's next date was no longer merely a date.…

On the morning of the next hearing, Delhi's sky was so blue that it seemed the night had tried, and failed, to wash away its crimes. Sunlight had not yet descended upon the old courthouse walls; smoke had. And the coconut leaves went on sounding through the night - kabaddi... name... kabaddi... name....

That night no dogs barked in Garh Narikel. Cats climbed onto the roofs and sat silent. The novel did not end in Channa Grove that night - only one cycle ended, with many more still to come. Its first circle was complete. The leaves moved, and those who had ears could hear: now the real story has begun.

At daybreak Batuknath Hariharan first demanded a towel to cover the water inside his house, then scolded the servant, then checked the tap, then the roof. When everything proved sound and yet water continued to drip from beneath his pillow, he understood that some things cannot be repaired by a workman. At dawn a leaf in Channa Grove moved lightly. Budhba Ghost looked down from his branch and whispered, "This is the mourning of victory. No court can impose a punishment greater than this grief."

On the fourth day after the third, the court opened again. The same doorway, the same metal detector, the same stairs, the same black coats, the same stale biscuits drowned in tea. When Batuknath arrived, the bench was clean. Yet he felt as though invisible people sat upon every bench. The court was no longer empty; it had filled with all those who had never received an entry pass.…

The seed of the names that had risen in dust upon the benches of the city's empty court travelled all night on the wind and reached Garh Narikel. Here the Court of Channa Grove had risen, yet its chairs remained. Ba said, "Yes. The school of names has opened."

After the archive of names is assembled, Garh Narikel asks how people—especially children—can resist the fear, shame and isolation produced by the screen. The answer takes institutional form as a school: justice is not only an order from a court, but also a shared practice of learning, asking and refusing to remain alone.

"You are not alone, are you?" That question had now become a greeting in the village. On the strength of it, once the Archive of Names had been made, people thought peace would at last descend upon the village. Devika stood at a distance and read it. She knew Ujjwal would not return. But now, if another Ujjwal became trapped, he would have somewhere to speak before dying. This was not justice, but it was the thing needed before justice: support.…

Dawn in Cambridge is not like dawn in Garh Narikel. There, mist does not rise over paddy fields, dew does not drip from the edges of coconut leaves, and the ghosts of Channa Grove do not end their night's kabaddi and climb back onto their branches. The following week Edward Broom changed the name of his company. The news spoke of a new beginning, a new commitment, a new ethical direction. The children of Garh Narikel laughed. Changing a name does not change a crocodile's teeth.…

chapters.s: Across the sea the stage had fallen empty and the company had changed its name; here in the city Batuknath Hariharan held the paper of victory, yet could find no taste of victory. The paper was thick, the seal shone, and the language of the order was so courteous that even cruelty wore manners. And in the city Batuknath Hariharan put his order of victory into a cupboard. Sunlight did not reach the document. Yet from inside the cupboard he sometimes heard the rustle of leaves. Each time he started.…

In the city cupboard the paper of victory had listened all night to the rustle of leaves; meanwhile in Garh Narikel the first thin light of dawn caught upon the branches of Channa Grove as though the night's court had not yet been adjourned.… And the village - Garh Narikel - begins again.
